blocks.text: Read the chapter with this setting in view: Isaiah contains the named prophet, divine speech, sign children, royal and national addressees, servants, heralds, Zion and Babylon as personified women, communal voices, and third-person prose narration; speaker identity must be established passage by passage. It gives a starting point for following the chapter's own movement. The chapter itself should determine how far the point is taken. The evidence leaves some details unresolved.

A literary feature to notice is that The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete sixty-six-chapter witness broadly aligned with the Masoretic tradition but containing thousands of orthographic and substantive differences; other Qumran Isaiah manuscripts and pesharim show active transmission and interpretation. This form helps organize the chapter's claims. Notice it before drawing broader conclusions from a single phrase or image. A more precise reconstruction remains disputed.
